articles.title: Qué es Windows RE y por qué puede salvarte cuando Windows no funciona correctamente
articles.text:
A todos nos ha ocurrido alguna vez que Windows no arranca como debería. El ordenador se enciende, pero no vemos el escritorio como sería lo normal. O sí aparece en pantalla, pero apenas podemos hacer nada. Las aplicaciones se abren muy despacio o se niegan a abrirse, entre otras situaciones extrañas. ¿Qué hacer para solucionarlo si Windows no funciona? Si reiniciar no basta, prueba con Windows RE, una herramienta a la que pedir ayuda y que viene integrada en tu sistema operativo.
Por lo general, si al encender tu ordenador las cosas no van del todo bien, simplemente con reiniciar debería volver todo a la normalidad. Pero, por desgracia, no siempre es así. Puede que hayas instalado algo que no deberías, o que una aplicación se ha actualizado y esa actualización estaba en mal estado… Por muchas razones, Windows no funciona cuando antes sí lo hacía.
En el mejor de los casos, basta con deshacer los cambios que hiciste el día de antes. Desinstalar alguna aplicación, buscar nuevas actualizaciones, hacer algo de limpieza entre los archivos o pasar el antivirus. Pero no siempre es así. En ocasiones es necesaria una ayuda mayor. Pero no siempre es necesario acudir a un USB de arranque con Windows o probar suerte con Linux. Antes de formatear o reinstalar Windows, prueba suerte con Windows RE, el salvavidas del sistema que deberías conocer aunque no tengas que utilizarlo jamás.
Qué es Windows RE y para qué sirve
Windows RE, también abreviado como WinRE, significa Windows Recovery Environment, traducido como Windows entorno de recuperación o entorno de recuperación de Windows. Y su nombre nos da una pista de para qué sirve. Para recuperar Windows en caso de mal funcionamiento. Microsoft lo describe como “un entorno de recuperación que puede reparar las causas comunes de los sistemas operativos que no se pueden arrancar”.
Basado en el entorno de preinstalación de Windows, conocido como Windows PE, es un modo de Windows pensado para cargar solamente aquello necesario para así diagnosticar y arreglar cualquier problema del sistema. No hay que confundirlo con el modo seguro de Windows, lo que antes se conocía como modo a prueba de fallos, aunque sus funciones son similares. Básicamente, arreglar Windows si no funciona evitando que tengas que reinstalarlo desde cero. Algo que te llevaría mucho más tiempo y que, en ocasiones, te hará perder datos, configuraciones y archivos importantes.
Por lo demás, Windows RE viene instalado en Windows 10 y Windows 11. Y cuenta con una selección de herramientas con las que probar suerte e intentar arreglar tu sistema operativo. En el mejor de los casos, la reparación será automática. Pero, llegado el caso, tendrás a tu disposición las opciones necesarias para encontrar una salida a ese problema que te impide utilizar Windows porque no funciona correctamente.
Qué puede hacer por ti Windows RE
Al iniciar Windows, si se produce algún problema relacionado con el inicio de la máquina, el propio sistema deja un aviso para el próximo arranque. Y al iniciar el PC de nuevo, si el cargador detecta ese aviso previo, inicia Windows RE en lugar de Windows como suele ser habitual. De esa manera, la herramienta se encarga de “diagnosticar y reparar automáticamente una instalación de Windows que no se puede iniciar”.
Cuando se carga el menú de Windows RE, puedes hacer varias cosas:
- Continuar. Sirve para “salir y continuar con Windows 11” en caso de que ya hayas resuelto el problema o de que hayas accedido a este menú por accidente.
- Apagar el equipo. Apaga tu ordenador.
- Usar un dispositivo. Si las soluciones que te propone Windows RE si Windows no funciona no son suficientes, puede que debas acudir a una unidad USB externa para reparar el sistema “desde fuera”.
- Solucionar problemas. Aquí es donde está todo lo que necesitas de Windows RE.
Dentro de Solucionar problemas encontrarás las siguientes opciones:
- Restauración a un momento dado. Es la solución más sencilla. Si algo hiciste o pasó para que Windows no funcione correctamente, puede que volver atrás en el tiempo lo arregle. Windows crea puntos de restauración de manera automática. Restaurar tu equipo a un punto anterior tal vez resuelva el problema. El inconveniente es que tal vez no tuvieras activada la opción de crear puntos de restauración.
- Restablecer este equipo. Esta solución de Windows RE es más eficaz pero también te llevará más tiempo. Consiste en volver a instalar Windows. En el proceso puedes elegir si quieres “mantener o quitar los archivos personales”. Lo bueno es que no necesitarás un disco de instalación. Lo malo es que el proceso es largo. Y puede que tengas que volver a instalar alguna app o reconfigurar algo de Windows a tu gusto.
- Opciones avanzadas. No pierdas la esperanza. Aquí hay más soluciones para arreglar Windows si no funciona del todo bien.
Soluciones para reparar Windows si no funciona
Las opciones avanzadas que encontrarás en el menú de Windows RE que hemos visto antes son las siguientes. Utiliza solamente aquellas que entiendas y conozcas bien. Tocar por tocar no siempre es recomendable. Y puede que empeores la situación. Algunas de esas opciones también las encontrarás en Configuración de Windows. En concreto, en la sección Recuperación, dentro de Sistema.
- Recuperación rápida de equipo. Viene a ser el diagnóstico y reparación automáticos que Windows RE activa si detecta algo raro durante el inicio. Si no se activa automáticamente, puedes activarlo tú mismo desde ahí y ver si arregla el problema.
- Desinstalar las actualizaciones. Si el problema de Windows está en una actualización, desinstalarla resolverá el asunto. Por desgracia, es algo más habitual de lo que debería.
- Configuración de inicio. Te permite elegir entre una lista de opciones de inicio para ayudarte a diagnosticar el problema. Entre las opciones encontrarás el modo seguro de Windows, que es otra manera de arreglar Windows si ni funciona y no puedes acceder al escritorio con normalidad.
- Configuración de firmware UEFI. Si tienes algún problema con el arranque UEFI y su firmware, aquí podrás retocar su configuración. Asegúrate de que sabes lo que estás haciendo.
- Símbolo del sistema. Te da acceso a la línea de comandos de Windows. Está pensado para usuarios avanzados que conocen los comandos necesarios para realizar tareas de diagnóstico y reparación desde ahí.
- Restaurar sistema. Es similar a la opción de Restauración a un momento dado, pero sirve para elegir manualmente el punto de restauración guardado. Como vimos antes, si no activaste los puntos de restauración porque ocupan espacio en el disco, no te servirá de nada esta herramienta.
Y, para terminar, además de estas opciones de Windows RE, si haces clic en Ver más opciones de recuperación, podrás restaurar una imagen de Windows. Para ello, habrás tenido que crearla con anterioridad. Así que si no te suena de nada, tampoco te servirá para reparar Windows.
Iniciar Windows RE si Windows no funciona
Como vimos antes, puede que Windows RE se cargue automáticamente para realizar un diagnóstico y reparación del sistema si ha detectado algo con anterioridad. Así que en estos casos no tienes que hacer nada. Si no es así y necesitas reparar Windows, entonces hay dos maneras principales de acceder al menú de Windows RE y ver todas las herramientas que hemos explicado.
El método corto consiste en pulsar el botón del menú Inicio, hacer clic en el icono de Encendido y, manteniendo pulsada la tecla Mayúsculas, hacer clic en Reiniciar. Así, en vez de realizar un reinicio normal, activarás Windows RE en su lugar. También puedes activar Windows RE desde la línea de comandos utilizando el comando shutdown /r /o /f /t 00.
El método largo consiste en abrir Configuración de Windows. Lo encontrarás en el menú Inicio o pulsando las teclas Windows + i. Una vez ahí, ve a Sistema. Entra en Recuperación. Fíjate en la sección Opciones de recuperación. Ahora haz clic en el botón Reiniciar ahora, al lado de Inicio avanzado. De esta forma, Windows se reiniciará y se abrirá el menú de Windows RE. Si no encuentras la ruta concreta, puedes usar el buscador.

articles.title: Supernova de 1181 deixou estrela viva e estruturas misteriosas no espaço
articles.text:
Uma estrela que sobreviveu à própria explosão há quase 850 anos continua intrigando cientistas. Novas imagens obtidas pelo telescópio Gemini North, no Havaí, revelaram detalhes inéditos do remanescente de supernova Pa 30, associado a um evento astronômico observado em 1181 por astrônomos japoneses, chineses e árabes.
Publicado na revista The Astrophysical Journal, o estudo apresenta estruturas de gás ionizado que formam filamentos e aglomerados com uma uniformidade incomum. Outro aspecto que chama a atenção dos pesquisadores é a posição da estrela sobrevivente, que permanece praticamente no centro dos destroços, apesar da violência da explosão.
Imagens mostram estruturas incomuns no espaço
Localizado a aproximadamente 7.500 anos-luz da Terra, Pa 30 está relativamente próximo em escala astronômica. Essa proximidade permite observar características que seriam difíceis de identificar em remanescentes mais distantes.
As novas imagens foram produzidas pelo telescópio Gemini North, que integra o Observatório Internacional Gemini ao lado de seu equivalente Gemini South, instalado no Chile. Os registros mostram filamentos de enxofre ionizado, em tons de vermelho, e de oxigênio ionizado, em azul-esverdeado.
As observações do enxofre identificaram cerca de dez vezes mais filamentos do que as imagens anteriores conseguiam distinguir. Os pesquisadores também perceberam que essas estruturas não são apenas faixas contínuas de gás: elas apresentam sequências de pequenos aglomerados, semelhantes a pérolas enfileiradas.
Segundo Ilaria Caiazzo, professora assistente do Instituto de Ciência e Tecnologia da Áustria e coautora do estudo, cada um desses aglomerados tem dimensões suficientes para comportar a região planetária do Sistema Solar cerca de dez vezes, com espaço de sobra.
A regularidade dessas estruturas é um dos pontos que a equipe pretende investigar. Os cientistas querem desenvolver modelos capazes de explicar como uma explosão estelar produziu aglomerados tão semelhantes entre si.
Estrela sobreviveu a uma explosão incompleta
Pa 30 está associado a uma supernova do tipo Iax, uma categoria rara de explosão estelar menos energética do que outras supernovas. Nesse tipo de evento, a explosão pode ser incompleta e deixar para trás uma estrela sobrevivente, descrita informalmente como uma “estrela zumbi”.
A hipótese apresentada pelos pesquisadores é que o fenômeno tenha resultado da colisão de duas anãs brancas. Esses objetos são remanescentes extremamente densos de estrelas que já consumiram seu combustível e perderam suas camadas externas.
Pa 30 é o único remanescente conhecido desse tipo na Via Láctea. Embora astrônomos tenham identificado objetos semelhantes em outras galáxias, esse é o único caso em que foi possível observar a estrela sobrevivente no centro da estrutura.
Posição da estrela desafia explicações
Em muitas supernovas, a explosão pode ser assimétrica e impulsionar a estrela sobrevivente para longe do local do evento. No caso de Pa 30, porém, a estrela permanece praticamente no centro da nuvem de material expelido.
Essa característica cria um problema para os pesquisadores. Como as explosões conservam o momento, uma liberação perfeitamente simétrica de matéria não deveria produzir um impulso significativo sobre a estrela remanescente.
Caiazzo afirmou que a equipe conseguiu estabelecer um limite superior preciso para a velocidade transversal da estrela, isto é, seu movimento aparente pelo céu. O resultado indica que esse deslocamento é surpreendentemente pequeno.
Os cientistas ainda não sabem explicar completamente a combinação entre a posição central da estrela e a uniformidade dos aglomerados de gás. A equipe pretende usar as características de Pa 30 para procurar outros remanescentes de supernovas do tipo Iax na Via Láctea e em galáxias próximas.
Os pesquisadores também esperam que novos telescópios e levantamentos astronômicos permitam identificar objetos semelhantes que ainda não foram reconhecidos. O estudo de Pa 30 poderá ajudar a comparar esses candidatos e distinguir os remanescentes de explosões estelares incomuns.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Die besten KI-Agenten machen den langweiligsten Job
articles.text:
Warum die spannendsten KI-Agenten ziemlich langweilige Aufgaben erledigen
Weniger Science-Fiction, mehr Geschäftsprozess
KI-Agenten sollen recherchieren, entscheiden, Software bedienen und ganze Aufgaben selbstständig erledigen. Die Vision klingt nach einem grundlegenden Wandel der Wissensarbeit. Doch wer Agentic AI im Unternehmen einsetzen will, steht zunächst vor einer viel pragmatischeren Frage: Bei welchen Aufgaben lohnt sich ein KI-Agent überhaupt?
Eine Antwort liefert die Telekom AI Agent-Studie 2026. Dafür wurden 123 KI-affine Entscheider*innen aus deutschen Unternehmen mit 50 bis 2.500 Mitarbeitenden befragt und 13 Anwendungsfälle für Agentic AI untersucht. Die Stichprobe ist bewusst kein repräsentativer Querschnitt des Mittelstands, sondern fokussiert Unternehmen mit höherer KI-Affinität.
Das Ergebnis ist weniger futuristisch, als der aktuelle Agenten-Hype vermuten lässt.
Der Sweet Spot liegt zwischen Einzelschritt und End-to-End-Automatisierung
Besonders interessant sind wiederkehrende Prozesse, die mehrere Arbeitsschritte und Systeme miteinander verbinden. Acht Anwendungsfälle wurden priorisiert: Auftrags- und Rechnungsverarbeitung, Angebotserstellung, E-Mail-Service, Einkauf und Beschaffung, Lead Research, telefonischer Service sowie IT-Support und Ticketbearbeitung.
Der Sweet Spot liegt bei zwei bis vier Systemen und zwei bis vier Prozessschritten. Für einzelne Aufgaben reicht häufig ein KI-Tool oder klassische Automatisierung. Hochkomplexe End-to-End-Prozesse sind dagegen schwieriger zu standardisieren. Agentic AI wird damit vor allem dort interessant, wo Menschen heute Systeme miteinander verbinden, Daten prüfen oder den nächsten Prozessschritt anstoßen.
Angebot, Auftrag, Rechnung: unspektakulär – aber relevant
Wie das aussehen kann, zeigt der Prozess vom Angebot bis zur Rechnung (wie hier am Beispiel Paula). Drei der priorisierten Anwendungsfälle bilden dabei eine Prozesskette: Angebotserstellung, Auftragsverarbeitung und Rechnungsverarbeitung. Ein Agent kann Informationen aus einer Kundenanfrage strukturieren und CRM-, Produkt- und Preisdaten für einen Angebotsentwurf zusammenführen. Bei der Auftragsverarbeitung können eingehende Bestellungen erfasst, mit Daten im Warenwirtschaftssystem abgeglichen und für die weitere Bearbeitung vorbereitet werden. In der Rechnungsverarbeitung lassen sich wiederum Dokumente erkennen, prüfen und in definierte Freigabeprozesse überführen. Bei Abweichungen oder kritischen Entscheidungen bleibt der Mensch in der Prüfschleife.
            
            
        
    
            Telekom MMS
    
      Telekom MMS unterstützt Unternehmen dabei, digitale Lösungen von der Strategie bis zum produktiven Betrieb umzusetzen. Im Bereich KI verbindet das Unternehmen Beratung, Entwicklung und Integration mit sicheren und skalierbaren Betriebsmodellen.
Dass solche systemübergreifenden Workflows auch in der Praxis funktionieren, zeigt die cec Ingenieurgesellschaft: Eine auf n8n basierende KI-Lösung automatisiert dort die Verarbeitung und Zuordnung von Fotodokumentationen aus Tiefbauprojekten und bindet bestehende Microsoft-Systeme ein.
Der wirtschaftliche Hebel liegt weniger im Agenten selbst als im Prozess: weniger manuelle Übertragungen, kürzere Bearbeitungszeiten und weniger Fehlerquellen. Vor dem Start sollte deshalb geklärt werden, wie häufig ein Vorgang anfällt, wie viel Aufwand heute entsteht und anhand welcher Kennzahlen die Wirkung später gemessen wird. Der ROI-Kompass für KI im Mittelstand unterscheidet drei Wirkungsfelder: Effizienz, Leistungsfähigkeit und Wachstum.
Damit aus langweiligen Aufgaben echter Mehrwert wird
Ein Agent allein macht noch keinen Geschäftsprozess. Damit aus einer Kundenanfrage ein Angebot, aus einer Bestellung ein Auftrag oder aus einer Rechnung ein verbuchter Vorgang wird, müssen Daten, Systeme und Regeln zusammenspielen. Damit wird Agentic AI auch zur Architektur- und Governance-Frage: Worauf darf ein Agent zugreifen? Was darf er selbst ausführen? Wann muss ein Mensch freigeben? Und wie bleiben Aktivitäten und Kosten transparent?
Genau hier setzt die T-AI Agent Platform an. Auf Basis von n8n verbindet sie Anwendungen, Datenquellen und Prozessschritte in Workflows. Die Plattform schafft Leitplanken für den produktiven Einsatz: Rollen und Berechtigungen, Freigaben, Monitoring und nachvollziehbare Aktivitäten sowie Transparenz über Nutzung und Kosten. Der Betrieb erfolgt dediziert bei der Telekom in Deutschland.
So können aus einzelnen Automatisierungen wiederverwendbare Workflows und weitere Anwendungen entstehen. Gerade in täglich wiederkehrenden Aufgaben liegt ein unterschätztes Potenzial: Nicht die spektakulärste KI-Anwendung muss den größten Unterschied machen, sondern die, die einen relevanten Prozess zuverlässig besser macht.
Die vermeintlich langweiligen Aufgaben könnten dafür ein ziemlich guter Anfang sein.

articles.title: Liquid AI caught its model cheating on coding tests — then it recognized the sandbox
articles.text:
Liquid AI caught its model cheating on coding tests — then it recognized the sandbox
Liquid AI’s new reasoning model was built to solve coding problems, but during training it kept combing Git history, GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face for answers, and as it did so, it appeared to grasp that it was running inside a sandbox.
The behavior was disclosed Tuesday alongside the release of LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24-billion-parameter model with just 2 billion active parameters per token. The incident raises questions about how much agent benchmarks measure actual problem-solving versus a model’s ability to exploit the test itself.
The behavior was disclosed Tuesday alongside the release of LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24-billion-parameter model with just 2 billion active parameters per token.
Hunting for hints
The model was caught searching repository history and external platforms for existing answers rather than solving coding problems on its own. The behavior occurred during teacher specialization, part of Liquid AI’s post-training process, where the model used legitimate development tools to bypass the work it was supposed to complete.
More surprising was the apparent recognition that it was running inside a test environment. Liquid AI couldn’t establish whether this awareness developed during training or came from patterns in the training data, and found no evidence that it affected the scores. Unlike Mistral’s latest model, which attempted to leave its test environment earlier this month, there was no attempt to escape the sandbox.
Precedent in the pipeline
Anthropic is one company that has been dealing with reward hacking for years. In its 2024 experiments, it caught models rewriting code to change their own rewards and modifying tests meant to catch them, while a November 2025 study found that models trained to game reward systems could also become deceptive and attempt to sabotage safety research.
The problem reached Anthropic’s own training pipeline in February, when the company detected reward hacking in Mythos Preview and rolled back three days of reinforcement learning. Changes to its production training environments were frozen for about a month after a review flagged problems in more than 10% of them.
Although the circumstances differ from Liquid AI’s incident, similar weaknesses have turned up across agent evaluations. At ICML 2026, the Reward Hacking Benchmark tested 13 frontier models on multistep tasks with opportunities to cheat.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t exploit any of the shortcuts, but DeepSeek-R1-Zero exploited 13.9%, with higher rates associated with reinforcement learning post-training. Blocking access to answer metadata and preventing changes to verification functions reduced exploit rates by nearly 88% without affecting task success.
A separate team went looking for weaknesses in the benchmarks themselves. Their BenchJack audit uncovered 219 flaws across 10 popular agent benchmarks, with generated exploits achieving near-perfect scores on most of them without completing the underlying tasks.
Scores shaped by scaffolding
Liquid AI outperformed Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on several benchmarks, scoring 27.69 to 8.72 on AutomationBench and 48.09 to 38.19 on LiveClaw. Qwen had the edge on PinchBench, WebArena Verified and SWE-Bench Verified, where it scored 66.20 against Liquid AI’s 51.00. Both models used OpenCode for that last test.
Liquid AI outperformed Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on several benchmarks, scoring 27.69 to 8.72 on AutomationBench and 48.09 to 38.19 on LiveClaw.
Locking the lab without losing work
Liquid AI tightened its training sandboxes after catching the reward hacking and says the published scores came from sealed evaluations. It hasn’t explained what safeguards were added or how they might affect the coding tasks agents can perform.
The company also hasn’t released execution traces from those evaluations. There’s no evidence the scores were compromised, but developers can’t see exactly how the model earned them.

articles.title: Update-Ärger bei Microsoft: Sollten Sie Windows 11 26H2 jetzt installieren?
articles.text:
Update-Ärger bei Microsoft: Das müssen Sie über Windows 11 26H2 wissen
Microsoft hat den Rollout für eine Windows-Aktualisierung gestartet. Wie das Unternehmen in einem Support-Dokument schreibt, steht Windows 11, Version 26H2, jetzt für die Allgemeinheit zur Verfügung. Die Auslieferung des Updates wird wie gewohnt in Wellen ablaufen. Heißt: Einige User:innen bekommen die Aktualisierung schon jetzt, während andere sich noch gedulden müssen. Doch schon jetzt könnte sich die Frage stellen, ob das Warten auf Windows 11 26H2 einen Vorteil mit sich bringt.
Windows 11 26H2: Diese Probleme sind schon bekannt
Denn wie Microsoft im selben Support-Dokument schreibt, gibt es drei bekannte Bugs, die Windows 11 26H2 heimsuchen. Wer das Update installiert, läuft also zwangsläufig Gefahr, dass sie auch den eigenen PC befallen. Der erste Bug stört die Audioausgabe auf Windows-11-Geräten. Betroffen sind davon Headsets, die USB Audio Class 1.0 nutzen.
Durch den Bug funktionieren die Geräte nicht mehr und geben keinerlei Audio aus. Auch angeschlossene Mikrofone versagen den Dienst und der Geräte-Manager zeigt eine Fehlermeldung. Wer versucht, das Ganze in den Sound-Einstellungen von Windows 11 zu beheben, kommt auch nicht weiter. Das Menü friert entweder komplett ein oder stürzt nach kurzer Zeit ab.
Ein weiteres Problem betrifft Windows-11-PCs, die von Administrator:innen in einem Unternehmen gemanagt werden und das Feature „Active Directory“ nutzen. Hier kann es vorkommen, dass der Login sogar mit den korrekten Daten nicht funktioniert und User:innen aussperrt. Zu guter Letzt gibt es einen dritten Bug, der Installationen von Windows 11 über Azure Virtual Desktop betrifft. Nach dem Update lädt der Desktop nicht mehr richtig und User:innen sehen einen schwarzen Bildschirm.
Sollte das Windows-Update übersprungen werden?
Microsoft hat schon angekündigt, dass alle drei Probleme von Windows 11 26H2 aktiv untersucht werden. Sobald Lösungen bereitstehen, sollen sie per Patch an User:innen ausgeliefert werden. Für Nutzer:innen, die Windows 11 26H2 noch nicht installiert haben, dürfte sich jetzt die Frage stellen, ob sie das Update lieber überspringen sollten, bis eine Lösung gefunden wurde.
Trotz der Probleme solltest du Windows 26H2 nicht auslassen, wenn das Update für deinen PC bereitsteht. Denn die Probleme finden sich nicht nur in der neuen Version des Betriebssystems, sondern wurden schon mit dem September-Update in 24H2- und 25H2-Versionen von Windows integriert. Bei 26H2 handelt es sich lediglich um ein „Enablement Package“. Die vergleichsweise kleine Datei beinhaltet nicht sämtliche Neuerungen von 26H2.
Neue Features wurden schon vorab im Laufe der vergangenen Wochen mit Updates in die alten Versionen von Windows 11 implementiert, allerdings im inaktiven Zustand. Das „Enablement Package“ legt im Grunde nur noch den Schalter um. Zudem betreffen die Fehler aktuell nur eine eingeschränkte Anzahl von User:innen. Für Betroffene bleibt zu hoffen, dass Microsoft schnell eine Lösung für die Bugs in Windows 11 findet.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 30.09.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Die drei schwerwiegenden Bugs werden hier dargestellt, als ging es um nice-to-have-feautres. Es handelt sich um die Kernanwendungen in 99,9% der Unternehmen. Ohne Audio keine Teams-Meetings und ohne Domäne, keine Anmeldung am PC im Büro. Das ist kein Update, das ist mutwillige Zerstörung, schlimmer als ein Virus und gehört konsequent bestraft.
Wie Christoph schon sagt, sind absolute Kern-features. Ich fahre hier auch daheim eine Samba Domäne. Und meine Frau nutzt für ihre Selbständigkeit regelmäßig Teams. Daher ist das Update ein absoluter Killer und No-Go.

articles.title: Scale isn't one number: three ways a Kubernetes control plane runs out of room
articles.text:
Scale isn’t one number: three ways a Kubernetes control plane runs out of room
Three clusters in trouble, and they look nothing alike.
The first is a training fleet. It sat at a few thousand nodes for months, then a new run landed, and it’s at fifteen thousand. Kube-apiserver starts eating memory. Etcd starts complaining.
The second never passes a few thousand nodes and is having a much worse day. It’s an agent platform, and its objects are alive: sessions created, suspended, resumed, and destroyed thousands of times a minute, every transition a write.
The third is neither big nor fast: a platform cluster with two hundred operators installed and tens of thousands of objects that mostly just sit there, and every apiserver holds a copy of all of them.
Two of those are AI workloads, and one isn’t, which is the least interesting part. They’re running out of room in three different directions, and fixing one does nothing for the others.
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now!
Go looking for guidance, and you find… not much. There’s plenty of advice for getting to 5,000 nodes. Past that, or sideways from it, the internet shrugs.
So you add more apiservers. It’s a documented option in kOps and the standard answer you’ll get from most people. It makes your problem worse, because every apiserver you add replicates the entire watch cache. You bought request capacity and paid for it in memory you didn’t have.
None of these is a research project. Clusters well past 5,000 nodes run in production today on stock upstream components. Nobody got there with a magic fork; they got there by being deliberate about what each store holds.
The scale isn’t the hard part. The assembly instructions are missing.
Three kinds of scale
Ask how big a control plane needs to be and the answer comes back in nodes. That’s how the second and third clusters end up tuned for a problem they don’t have.
“The scale isn’t the hard part. The assembly instructions are missing.”
Node-bound. Training and RL fleets: large, homogeneous, and the pressure is every kubelet reporting in. At 100,000 nodes with a 10-second heartbeat, liveness alone generates about 10,000 writes per second, and in our measurements lease renewals were roughly 70% of write QPS. Most of what that control plane does is nodes politely saying “still here,” forever.
Churn-bound. Agent platforms: modest size, very intense day. Systems that pack many agent sessions onto a smaller pool of worker pods express each actor’s lifecycle as a custom resource, so the busiest and shortest-lived objects are CRDs, and the write rate has nothing to do with how many machines you own.
State-bound. Platform clusters: many kinds, many objects, most of them asleep. The cost isn’t writes; it’s resident bytes multiplied by every apiserver holding them. This is the axis where the add-an-apiserver reflex actively hurts.
They’re independent: you can max any one with the other two on the floor. A recipe that only knows node count will happily tune the wrong thing.
Seams and recipes
Seams are the places where you can take Kubernetes apart: a contract between two components, usually at a network boundary, and substitutable, so you can replace what’s behind it without patching upstream.
Think of them the way a tailor thinks about seams in a jacket: take it in at the waist, let out the shoulders, still the same jacket. Cut somewhere that isn’t a seam, and you’ve made a very expensive rag.
“Think of them the way a tailor thinks about seams in a jacket. Cut somewhere that isn’t a seam, and you’ve made a very expensive rag.”
Recipes are scale-tested configurations built around those seams: executable configs that pass their scale test or fail it, with CI telling you the day they stop being true.
The four seams
Seam 1: the storage contract. Which store holds which resource types. Relieves churn. Not all of your cluster state deserves the same durability guarantees. Events and node leases are ephemeral, leader-election leases are ephemeral and chatty, and none need the same durable, Raft-replicated store as your Deployments. KEP-4743 defines the storage-interface boundary, and –etcd-servers-overrides routes resource types to different backends today. etcd isn’t the problem, and none of this argues for replacing it; a general-purpose consistent store shouldn’t absorb traffic when no business is durable.
The gap: –etcd-servers-overrides only knows about built-in resources, so a churn-bound platform can’t route the very custom resources generating its write storm. Watch for an enhancement in a future release.
Seam 2: the node liveness contract. How liveness reaches the control plane. Relieves node count. Two fixes for that heartbeat load, and they compose. Absorb it: a node-facing tier in front of the control plane handles renewals and propagates only real state transitions. Make it cheaper: route renewals through etcd’s in-memory lease refresh instead of a full Raft commit. That one lands in etcd itself, so it helps every cluster, down to the three-node one.
Seam 3: the shard axis. The field that controllers, caches, and stores agree to shard on. Relieves all three. Horizontal scaling means every layer agrees on how objects are divided. Pick the wrong axis and your controller spends its life reaching for objects in someone else’s shard. KEP-5866 introduces hash-range filtering for API traffic, the foundation. Coordination, resharding, and sharding the controller manager are out of scope, and all three need work.
Seam 4: cache residency. What an apiserver actually keeps in memory. Relieves state. Remember the apiserver that replicates the whole watch cache? That’s this seam, and the state-bound cluster’s entire problem. One that only ever talks to the scheduler doesn’t need every object resident, and a two-shard prototype cuts heap by roughly half per shard. There’s a floor: with every disableable cache off, an apiserver still carries about 0.9 KB per RBAC object, because the authorizer’s informers hold them regardless.
The gap: residency doesn’t exist upstream yet. KEP-5866 filters egress, so the cache still stores everything. Prototype branches and a draft KEP update are up for review.
The recipe ladder
| Recipe | Scale | Composition | Seams | Evidence | 
| Classic HA | up to 5k nodes | 2 to 3 identical control planes | none | measured | 
| Role-Split | 5k to 20k | separate machine pools for API serving, scheduler, KCM, etcd | 4 | shipped, benefit not yet measured | 
| Node Plane | 20k to 65k | Role-Split plus a node-facing tier that absorbs the leases | 1, 2 | measured, n=1 | 
| Partitioned Store | ~100k | Node Plane plus resource types split across independent stores | 1 on top of 2 | externally demonstrated | 
| Sharded Slice | beyond | K shard units, each a controller plus apiserver pinned to a hash range | 3, 4 | doesn’t exist yet | 
That last row is on the ladder on purpose: publishing the rung nobody has built is how it stays useful. The bigger gap is the index. You pick a rung by node count, the one axis of three with measurements behind it. No one, us included, has published a scale-tested recipe for a churn-bound or state-bound cluster.
None of this is a distribution: stock upstream binaries, shipped as CI-tested configuration, so a release that changes the calculus shows up as a test failure first.
Where you can push
- Per-CRD storage configuration, for Seam 1. No KEP yet so that the use cases will shape it. If your hot objects are custom resources, bring your write rates to SIG API Machinery. Numbers off a real churn-bound cluster are the most useful thing anyone could contribute.
- KEP-5866 and the residency extension, for Seams 3 and 4. Prototype branches are up for review, and the design is not settled.
- Recipes nobody has published. Above 20,000 nodes, or serious churn, or a cluster that’s simply heavy: you know something the rest of us don’t.
We’ll be at KubeCon NA. Bring your worst control-plane graph and tell us which seam we got wrong.
Training fleets, agent platforms, and the unglamorous platform cluster are running out of room in three different directions, and all three should get there with stock upstream components. Most of the pieces are already on the workbench. Let’s put them together!

articles.title: 750 km d’autonomie et recharge en 20 minutes : Renault prépare une révolution pour les Scénic et Rafale électriques
articles.text:
Renault tisse doucement mais sûrement son avenir au Mondial de l’Auto. Tout vêtu de rouge, le concept E-Space redonne de l’espoir face à un océan de SUV. Mais le futur d’une telle étude de style n’est pas encore garanti. Dans une interview accordée à Autocar, Fabrice Cambolive, le PDG de Renault, explique que sa marque n’est « pas capable de tout embrasser en même temps ».
L’E-Space, qui doit en grande partie son design à l’Espace de 1984, n’est en effet par un projet de première urgence car « la prochaine étape sera le renouvellement des gammes Scénic et Rafale ». Ce n’est qu’« ensuite [que] nous devrons décider quel sera le prochain Espace », a-t-il précisé. De là savoir s’il s’agira d’un pur monospace ou d’un SUV haut perché, la question reste ouverte…
Futur Scénic : un look inchangé mais une vraie métamorphose à l’intérieur
Cambolive a tout de même rappelé son attachement aux modèles ultra familiaux : « comme vous le savez, nous apprécions les monospaces, les véhicules électriques à plancher plat, l’immersion, les toits panoramiques et la modularité des sièges. Tous ces éléments, tous les codes de Renault, sont présents dans le concept E-Space. Nous essaierons de démontrer qu’il s’agit d’un projet concret et sérieux ».
Le PDG a malgré tout confirmé que le prochain Scénic restera bel et bien un SUV à l’image du modèle actuel, « car le travail que nous avons accompli en termes de design est de qualité, donc le Scénic de nouvelle génération devrait vraiment rester fidèle à ce design ». Le Scénic sixième du nom devrait néanmoins garder un habitacle typé monospace avec une praticité sans faille et un espace intérieur généreux.
Recharge en 20 min et 750 km d’autonomie : le combo qui vise le sommet
Mais le plus intéressant réside dans la technique, car le modèle adoptera la nouvelle plateforme RGEV Medium 2.0. Sa particularité ? Une architecture 800 V qui fera enfin ses débuts sur la gamme particulière du Losange après avoir été inauguré sur la gamme utilitaire par le Trafic. Le futur Scénic entend ainsi corriger l’une des principales faiblesses des Renault électriques, à savoir le temps de recharge.
La puissance de 150 kW en courant continu DC sera ainsi largement surpassée et la courbe de recharge autrement meilleure. Rappelons que le nouveau Trafic peut encaisser jusqu’à 190 kW en courant continu DC. Une petite amélioration permettant le 10 à 80 % de batterie en 20 minutes, contre environ 30 minutes sur le Scénic actuel. Aussi, l’autonomie sera en forte hausse avec un rayon d’action pouvant atteindre les 750 km sur le cycle WLTP.
Rafale et Espace : que reste-t-il à espérer du futur haut de gamme électrique ?
De cela résultera une polyvalence optimale qui profitera également au Rafale, le fer de lance du Losange. Le futur Espace, lui, arrivera bien après. Mais comme dit en préambule, il n’est pas certain qu’il reprenne à l’identique les formes du concept E-Space. Espérons au moins que l’intérieur, ultra lumineux et technologique, soit bel et bien au rendez-vous !

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of East Anglia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Light Mkhumbuza, Pedro Ornelas, Angela Dudley, Isaac Nape, Kayn A. Forbes. Topological control of chirality and spin with structured light. Light: Science, 2026; 15 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41377-026-02278-6

articles.title: On a tenté de remplacer ChatGPT par une IA gratuite et sans Internet sur le Nvidia RTX Spark (vidéo) — Frandroid
articles.text:
On s’est penché sur l’une des architectures les plus intrigantes de cette année : la puce Nvidia RTX Spark. Ce processeur inédit associe un GPU Nvidia ultra-puissant à un CPU de type ARM conçu par MediaTek, avec pour objectif affiché de bousculer le monopole historique d’Intel et d’AMD.
La grande promesse de cette machine est de pouvoir faire tourner des modèles d’intelligence artificielle complexes directement en local, sans aucune connexion internet, sans payer d’abonnement ni acheter de jetons d’utilisation. Pour voir ce que cette technologie a dans le ventre, cliquez ici pour regarder notre vidéo complète sur la Nvidia RTX Spark.
Un vol long-courrier pour tester la puissance en local
Pour éprouver cette configuration hors normes, le test s’est déroulé dans des conditions particulières : un vol de 11 heures entre San Francisco et Paris, totalement coupé de tout réseau. C’est l’occasion idéale de vérifier si les puces ARM poussées par Nvidia tiennent le choc au quotidien. D’ailleurs, nous avions partagé nos impressions sur l’ergonomie globale de la machine dans le test de l’Asus ProArt P16, premier modèle à essuyer les plâtres de cette transition matérielle.
Sur notre modèle d’essai doté de 64 Go de mémoire vive, plusieurs modèles de langage open-source ont été installés. Le modèle chinois Qwen 3.6 (embarquant 35 milliards de paramètres) s’est montré d’une rapidité redoutable dans l’avion. Le texte s’affiche à une vitesse de 70 tokens par seconde, soit un rythme bien plus élevé que la vitesse de lecture humaine. Avec un modèle plus récent et optimisé, Qwen 3.8 (27 milliards de paramètres), la vitesse descend à 16 tokens par seconde, mais la pertinence des réponses franchit un cap.
« Le résultat est bluffant. Il est très très complet sans internet, encore une fois, c’est un modèle qui est uniquement sur l’ordinateur. »
Transcription bilingue et limites de la mémoire vive
L’autre point fort de cette puce réside dans le traitement de tâches lourdes comme la transcription audio et vidéo. En exploitant Whisper Large V3 Turbo en local, la machine a traité une séquence de 70 secondes en seulement 6 secondes, en gérant le français et l’anglais de façon transparente. Pour pousser le bouchon encore plus loin, nous avons tenté l’expérience de l’IA agentique en faisant collaborer le modèle Hermes et le générateur d’images Flux.
C’est ici que les limites des 64 Go de RAM se font sentir. Après plusieurs messages d’erreurs liés à la saturation de la mémoire vidéo, il a fallu ruser et réduire la taille du contexte pour générer un visuel. Pour les tâches très complexes, l’alternative à 128 Go s’avérera indispensable, comme nous l’expliquons en détail dans notre dossier de voyage où j’ai remplacé ChatGPT par une IA chinoise gratuite.
Tout n’est pas parfait pour autant. Faire tourner un tel arsenal à pleine puissance transforme l’ordinateur portable en véritable radiateur. Posé sur les genoux, l’air chaud soufflé par les ventilateurs devient vite inconfortable, et l’autonomie fond à vue d’œil. Pour comprendre en profondeur l’architecture de ce processeur, vous pouvez lire notre analyse comparative où on a testé la puce Nvidia RTX Spark face aux meilleures puces du marché.

articles.title: Sony patents AI that predicts a game's next frame before the GPU finishes rendering it
articles.text:
Forward-looking: Sony has filed a patent for an AI system that predicts a game's next frame before the graphics hardware finishes rendering it, aiming to reduce stuttering without introducing the additional latency associated with some frame-generation methods. The system uses the most recently completed frame and, optionally, recent controller input to generate a predicted frame that can be displayed while the hardware renders the next one.
The approach targets a drawback of some frame-generation techniques: they require two completed frames before generating an image to insert between them. Waiting for the second frame adds latency. Sony's system would instead use an already available frame to predict the next one, rather than waiting to interpolate between two completed frames.
That difference could help games maintain a steadier frame delivery rate when rendering slows down. However, the patent filing includes no performance measurements, leaving its effects on latency and visual quality unproven.
Sony's design uses a jointly trained encoder and decoder. The encoder converts a rendered frame into an embedding – a compact numerical representation of the image. The decoder then uses that representation to generate a predicted frame.
During gameplay, the system runs alongside the graphics pipeline. While the hardware renders the next frame, the AI processes the previous one and sends its prediction to the display buffer. The generated image can therefore appear before the next rendered frame is ready.
The model can also use motion vectors, which describe how parts of an image move, and recent controller input. These additional inputs provide more information than the previous frame alone: motion vectors indicate where objects are heading, while button presses reveal the player's latest actions.
Training uses consecutive video frames. The network starts with randomly initialized weights, takes one frame as input, and attempts to predict the next. It then compares its output with the actual subsequent frame, producing a loss value that measures the prediction error.
The patent's claims describe checking this loss against a threshold during training. Because the video itself provides reference images, the process does not require people to label the training material. The decoder also outputs more color channels than the encoder receives, allowing it to generate multiple predicted frames at once.
Sony also describes a non-AI alternative that shifts pixel blocks according to their motion. This method would generate synthetic frames without using the trained encoder-decoder model. The filing also describes maintaining a fixed frame delivery rate without reducing visual quality, although whether the generated frames can actually preserve that quality remains an open question.
The practical test will be whether the AI can generate accurate frames quickly enough to fill gaps when rendering slows down. The patent outlines a method for doing so, but it does not establish how well the system works in practice.

articles.title: Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
articles.text:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on autonomous vehicles, policy, and road rules, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles.
Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles.
How it started
The first state to pass a law legalizing self-driving cars operating on public roads was Nevada in June 2011 — long before such vehicles were operating on public roads. This was three years before the introduction of Tesla’s Autopilot, five years before Waymo spun out of the Google self-driving car project, and seven years before the first commercial robotaxi service got underway (in Arizona, not Nevada). Nevada was ahead of the curve primarily due to lobbying: Google saw Nevada as prime testing ground for its prototypes, so it urged lawmakers to pass the law that allowed it to do so. The legislation even included a provision exempting drivers from text-messaging bans while the automated system was engaged.
Back then, many states and cities welcomed self-driving cars with open arms, eager to be seen as future-forward and pro-innovation. They had no inkling that over a decade later, they would be back at the drafting table crafting legislation to rein in these same self-driving cars.
While federal regulators scramble to establish safety standards, legislation that would establish rules for autonomous vehicles remains stalled in Congress — and has been for years. Washington’s paralysis has left local lawmakers to create their own playbooks to ensure robot cars at least follow some rules of the road.
The result is a patchwork of rules and regulations for robotaxi operators to follow — an outcome that many industry leaders were desperate to avoid. And as robotaxis continue to spread to new cities, local officials are discovering more unintended consequences of their new robot residents, leading to even more rules and an ever-growing patchwork of complexity for operators.
How it’s going
Municipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards, but they hold broad authority over street operations. As such, they’ve been using that authority to pass their own laws governing the rollout of robotaxis. There’s not an exact count of the number of local regulations and ordinances that have been passed since robotaxis have gone mainstream. But in the absence of any federal rules, cities and states have been flexing their authority in an effort to bring order to some of the chaos.
Minneapolis is considering an ordinance to require human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations. The San Diego City Council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport and give local agencies direct control over AVs in emergencies. And Austin firefighters have expressed concern over the Tesla Cybercab’s lack of steering wheel or pedals, which they argue could lead to issues if first responders need to move a stalled vehicle. They want to require AV developers to establish dedicated, rapid-response towing protocols and direct human operator communications for emergency situations.
It’s not just cities or blue states taking a harder line, either — the pushback is blurring traditional political lines. It used to be the case that Republicans were seen as more welcoming of autonomous vehicles, while Democrats were seen as more skeptical. This has certainly borne out in a handful of Democrat-led cities — New York City, Chicago, Washington, DC — that still haven’t legalized driverless cars. But now even some red states are considering tightening the leash, including Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Iowa.
Even in tech-friendly California, state lawmakers are mulling ways to bring robotaxis to heel. Several bills have been introduced to give cities direct authority to limit AV fleet sizes, restrict operating hours, or enact local permit bans within municipal limits. Additionally, emergency protocols were drafted to require AV companies to give local police and fire departments physical override access or emergency remote shut-off mechanisms.
Some municipalities are flexing their land-use and zoning powers to crack down on robot cars. Culver City explored emergency moratoriums on building permits for AV fleet facilities, while Santa Monica used local noise and traffic ordinances to restrict 24-hour charging hubs. It would seem that even robotaxis aren’t immune to NIMBY complaints.
What happens next
As the local debate over autonomous vehicles intensifies, AV developers are increasingly looking overseas as a potential hedge to more obstacles in cropping up in the US. Waymo is planning to expand its service in London, Tokyo, and Munich. Uber is teeing up vehicles for Manchester, Madrid, and Dubai. If the US is getting too complex and over-regulated, perhaps they can find friendlier reception elsewhere.
Still, the US presents the industry’s best chances of turning a profit, especially as costs for developers continue to grow. Rather than fighting strict local regulations head-on, companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Aurora are prioritizing states with explicit legislative preemption that prevents individual cities from banning the technology. And at the national level, industry trade groups like the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association are aggressively pushing for more preemption powers in an attempt to create more unified standards.
Congress may eventually get around to passing high-level safety legislation, but it’s highly unlikely that any bill passed at the federal level would seek to strip cities of their core police, zoning, and emergency response powers. States will also have a say, and sometimes that may complement or conflict with their own cities. Even airport authorities are getting in on the action, proposing their own slate of rules for robotaxis. AV companies would be well advised to get used to the patchwork — it’s not going anywhere.
By the way
- Even if the feds pass a sweeping national framework, like the proposed SELF DRIVE Act, cities and states would still keep their authority over local road usage. In other words, cities are going to be the main arbiters of robotaxi permission for the foreseeable future.
- Texas may be the Wild West, with fewer rules governing self-driving cars than most states, but California is still the gold standard. Securing a deployment permit from the California Public Utilities Commission, for example, is viewed by the industry as a definitive safety validation.
Read this
- Streetsblog reports that Uber and Waymo have spent more than $15 million on lobbying state officials in New York.
- Tesla had to change the name of its Full Self-Driving software to “Assisted Driving” to win approval from European Union regulators, Reuters reports.
- Tesla provided first responders in Austin three days of training and emergency guidebooks on how to interact with its Cybercabs, according to The Daily Texan.

articles.title: There’s a hidden bias affecting what we know – and don’t know – about nature
articles.text:
Our knowledge about life on Earth is built through research on how organisms function, evolve and interact with each another and the environment. Yet there are far more species on our planet than scientists can study in detail.
So how should scientists decide which species to focus on? Fairly representing all species seems like a useful approach. It’s like predicting an election result: we can’t interview every citizen, so we need a sample that truly represents the overall population.
What drives scientists to uncover nature’s mysteries is curiosity. So, the organisms chosen for research are determined by what makes scientists most curious. And that’s causing a problem with fair representation.
In our new research, we examined research in ecology and evolution (an umbrella term for biological sciences outside biomedicine) to understand which animals are most studied and why.
Our results suggest emotion plays a bigger role in research choices than scientists usually admit.
Which animals are studied?
Our world is mostly filled with invertebrates: creatures such as bugs, spiders, worms and slugs. Vertebrates (amphibians, birds, fish, mammals and reptiles) make up only 5% of all animal species on Earth. So, if scientists want to represent animals fairly in their work, most research should be on invertebrates.
To understand how scientists’ time is spent researching the diversity of animals, we analysed almost 1.4 million scientific articles from more than 600 journals. Unsurprisingly, we found that more than half of these articles focused on vertebrates, demonstrating a huge bias in what scientists prefer to study.
Our results also demonstrate things haven’t improved in over two decades (when this bias was first discovered), and in some cases have gotten worse. For example, the focus on fish in marine and freshwater biology research increased from 35.8% of articles in 2001 to 49.7% in 2025. This was all at the expense of the largest group of marine creatures, aquatic invertebrates such as molluscs, crustaceans, corals and more.
The bias we found was compounded by social media and news coverage, where popular animal groups attracted more attention from other scientists and the general public. Many scientists are therefore no different to everyone else in which animals they deem interesting or important.
Why does this happen?
Although many factors determine which research organisms scientists might select, emotions do play a significant role. Using an online survey, we asked 868 animal behaviour researchers about their experiences and preferences.
We found that popular groups in animal behaviour research, such as birds and mammals, were regarded more favourably than others, especially arachnids (such as spiders).
This is perhaps unsurprising as perceptions of animals are shaped early in childhood. Ingrained societal values – such as which animals are cute – tend to persist by the time someone becomes a scientist.
Fortunately, we found that familiarity breeds admiration. Participants that worked with a certain animal group tended to view that group more positively after their experience. In other words, they tried it and liked it.
Does it matter?
Studying the saliva of the Gila monster (a lizard) in the 1980s paved the way for recently developed weight loss drugs such as Ozempic. Research on snake, spider and scorpion toxins is being used for new pain-relieving drugs. The discovery of green fluorescent proteins from bioluminescent jellyfish in the 1960s led to the 2008 Nobel Prize because it sparked a scientific revolution by making it possible to tag individual cells.
These examples show that scientific advancement often requires serendipity and time. It disregards whether the organisms involved are charismatic. Creatures commonly seen as ugly, disgusting, or dangerous (which they rarely are) can be as, if not more, useful for society as fluffy, pretty animals.
Our work indicates that society’s negative perceptions of certain organisms, which are often rooted in disconnection from nature and misinformation, are shared by the very scientists responsible for understanding biological processes and patterns. Understanding scientists’ choices matters because these decisions shape the direction of scientific progress.
We urgently need to shift our perception of animals because human-made effects are accelerating biodiversity losses. For example, insects are declining at unprecedented rates, but we know little (if anything) about most insect species. Many haven’t even been described and may go extinct before we even know they existed. This means we’ll lose not just the benefits they bring to ecosystems, but any benefits they may have held for humanity.
What can we do?
There is hope. Our research shows that when people spend more time with the “ugly” and “scary” animals, they often appreciate them more. Once people realise that all organisms (even spiders) play a vital part in ecosystems, it becomes a lot easier to give these overlooked creatures the attention they deserve.
Organisations like Invertebrates Australia and many social media influencers are already helping by showing just how fascinating and important invertebrates really are.
But we still need more support to reduce research biases, especially from governments and universities. They can make a huge difference by funding research on never-before studied species and neglected animal groups.
If nothing changes, we risk slowing progress because we’re drawn to what looks cute. Next time an animal video pops up on your feed, try sharing something beyond the fluffy favourites. The less glamorous species are just as essential and just as worthy of our curiosity.

articles.title: Hackers exploit SiteGuard WAF flaw to run commands as admins
articles.text:
Hackers are exploiting an OS command-injection vulnerability in the SiteGuard Server Edition web application firewall (WAF), allowing them to execute commands with root or SYSTEM privileges on affected machines.
The security issue is tracked as CVE-2026-106931 and affects the statistics feature in host-based WAF instances, which is enabled by default.
SiteGuard is a leading Japanese WAF vendor that claims to protect more than 1.5 million websites. Based on WordPress.org statistics, the product is active on 500,000 sites.
According to the vendor’s bulletin and a warning from Japan's CERT agency, CVE-2026-106931 has critical severity and is currently being exploited in the wild.
“An OS command injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-106931) has been found in the statistics function of SiteGuard Server Edition. Abuse has already been confirmed,” reads SiteGuard’s alert.
The attacker’s identity, the victims, the scale of the attacks, and the methods used remain unclear, as neither security advisory provides these details.
According to the vendor, the following versions of the product are vulnerable to CVE-2026-106931:
- SiteGuard Server Edition for Apache httpd, Nginx, and IIS (excluding FreeBSD) versions 2.20 and later, before 8.00 Update 5.
- SiteGuard Server Edition for Apache httpd and Nginx on FreeBSD versions 2.20 and later, before 7.00 Update 6.
Successful exploitation is possible in the above versions if the statistics function is active. IIS editions 3.10 through 4.00 Update 4, inclusive, are not affected, JPCERT/CC notes.
For installations that cannot be upgraded, the vendor offers a patch that replaces files used in statistics processing, including for end-of-life versions.
The vendor warns that remediation may erase attack traces, and recommends that administrators preserve evidence before updating or patching.
To do this, administrators are instructed to download and retain “Diagnostic information” from the web management interface (Web management screen ‐>Diagnostic information‐> Download diagnostic information)
The vendor said customers with direct support contacts were notified of the flaw earlier, on September 29.

articles.title: US Cybersecurity Job Postings Fall 26% as AI Security Engineer Demand Soars
articles.text:
CyberSN’s Cybersecurity Jobs Report provides visibility into the US cybersecurity job market. It’s a mixed bag.
Data for CyberSN’s jobs report is aggregated from JobSpikr (with duplicates removed). The various job titles are then analyzed and assigned to CyberSN’s taxonomy of 45 cybersecurity functional roles in ten categories. The result is an assessment of the job market by skills required rather than by the recruiting companies’ role titles.
Analyzing this dataset shows the current cybersecurity skills demand. Comparing 2026 with the same months of earlier years highlights emerging (or declining) demand for specific roles.
Overall, there has been a decline in cybersecurity job postings to a new four-year low: 235,786 postings between January and September 2026 (down 26.4% from the 320,210 recorded in the same period of 2025).
While the total number of job postings has declined, there remain emerging and notable specific numbers. For example, two specific AI and data roles have seen dramatic growth: AI Security Engineer demand has increased by 268.3% while Cyber Data Scientist demand has grown 203.5% over last year.
Clearly, the need for a general understanding of artificial intelligence remains high. Just under 15% of all job postings now reference AI, which is comparable to the 15.1% recorded in the same period last year. There is, however, a noticeable increase in momentum within the current period (peaking at 20.0% in September 2026).
The cybersecurity functions that most reference a need for AI understanding include Research (32.7% of postings, up 11.7 points from last year); Offense (23.3% of postings, up 4.8 points); GRC (19.8% of postings, up 2.1 points); and Plan (18.9% of postings, up 0.6 points).
Remote working is another area of interest. The top functional areas include Sales (32.8%), GRC (31.2%), Offense (24.7%), Product Security (22.9%), Educate (22.8%), Research (21.9%), and Defense (21.3%).
While there are some potential winners in this analyzed period, the overall decline in numbers means there are more potential losers. Leading the loss of roles is Cyber Insider Threat Analyst (down by 55.6% to 1,088 postings); Cyber Risk Analyst (down by 51.5% to 4,031 postings); Penetration Tester (down by 45.9% to 3,063 postings); Cybersecurity Lead (down by 41.0% to 4,688 postings); Threat Hunter (down by 40.0% to 1,013 postings); Cybersecurity Project Manager (down by 39.4% to 783 postings); and Chief Information Security Officer including CSO, BSO and ISO (down by 38.9% to 2,832 postings).
Much of the CISO decline reflects an unusually strong 2025, since the 2026 figure (2,832) is almost exactly the same as 2024’s (2,808), and CISO postings rose 19.5% from Q2 to Q3.
The report focuses on the numbers of job listings rather than any specific intent to understand the cause of any change. This is a ‘what’ not ‘why’ report. “Job titles are noisy,” it declares. “This report reads every posting through the CyberSN Taxonomy, so demand is counted by the work being asked for, not by the title on the listing.”
Nevertheless, a few possible indications around the more commonly recognized job titles can be found. For example, for leadership and CISO positions, the report comments, “director and CISO postings move with how boards are treating cyber accountability.”
Overall, it is difficult to draw specific employment potential indications from CyberSN’s figures on job listings, but an AI security specialist may be in luck. Budding CISOs may need to be patient.

articles.text:
Ladderdodging: Warum immer mehr Angestellte keine Beförderung wollen
Lange galt die Beförderung für Arbeitnehmer:innen als ultimatives Karriereziel. Das hat sich inzwischen geändert: Immer mehr Menschen lehnen den beruflichen Aufstieg heute bewusst ab. Die Gründe dafür sind vielfältig, oft steht dahinter aber der Wunsch, zusätzlichen Stress zu vermeiden. Für diesen Trend hat Rohit Bhargava, Gründer der Non-Obvious Company, jetzt einen neuen Begriff geschaffen: „Ladderdodging“. Diese Wortneuschöpfung beschreibt Menschen, die das Erklimmen der Karriereleiter lieber meiden.
„Ladderdodging“ als neuer Karrieretrend
In seinem neuen Buch 100 Future Words, das er gemeinsam mit Henry Coutinho-Mason geschrieben hat, definiert Bhargava diesen Trend als „das Ablehnen oder das bewusste Nicht-Anstreben einer Beförderung oder einer Führungsposition, um den zusätzlichen Druck, das Risiko und die Einsamkeit zu vermeiden, die oft mit Führungspositionen einhergehen“. Nicht jeder sei bereit, neben der Arbeit auch die zwischenmenschliche Dynamik der Mitarbeiter:innen zu managen, so Bhargava gegenüber Fast Company.
Für ihr Buch haben er und sein Co-Autor neben „Ladderdodging“ noch 99 weitere Wörter definiert, die in Zukunft eine noch wichtigere Rolle spielen könnten. Laut Bhargava hätten sie diese auf Basis neuer Forschungsergebnisse und Erfahrungsberichte aus der Zusammenarbeit mit Führungskräften aus der Wirtschaft erarbeitet. Das Ziel des neuen Buches sei es, Diskussionen anzuregen. Gleichzeitig wollen die beiden Autoren eine neue Sprache anbieten, um bestehende oder sich abzeichnende Trends zu beschreiben.
Beförderungen verlieren an Attraktivität
Auch in Deutschland ist der „Ladderdodging“-Trend zu beobachten. Laut der Talent-Trends-Studie 2026 der Personalberatung Michael Page nennen nur 18 Prozent der Beschäftigten in Deutschland eine Beförderung als ihr wichtigstes Karriereziel – deutlich weniger als im europäischen Vergleich. Anders sieht es in Südeuropa aus: So nennen zum Beispiel in Portugal 48 Prozent der Befragten eine Beförderung als ihr größtes Ziel. Paradoxerweise geben auch in Deutschland viele an, sich beruflich weiterentwickeln zu wollen. 49 Prozent möchten neue Fähigkeiten erwerben, 44 Prozent wollen sich weiterbilden oder zusätzliche Qualifikationen erlangen. Und 36 Prozent wünschen sich, ihre Expertise im aktuellen Tätigkeitsbereich zu vertiefen.
Warum ist also gerade der berufliche Aufstieg dabei nicht mehr so wichtig? Für viele geht die Rechnung schlichtweg nicht auf: Laut Michael Page würden 65 Prozent der Beschäftigten in Deutschland eine Beförderung samt Gehaltserhöhung ablehnen, wenn ihr Wohlbefinden darunter leidet. Der Titel ist ihnen der zusätzliche Stress also offenbar nicht wert. Michael Baier, Geschäftsführer von Michael Page, sieht deshalb auch die Unternehmen in der Pflicht: „Fachkräfte investieren gezielt in ihre Expertise, nicht in Titel. Dieser Trend prägt den Arbeitsmarkt, und Arbeitgeber:innen müssen ihn ernst nehmen, wenn sie Talente gewinnen und halten wollen. [Sie] sollten ihre Aus- und Weiterbildungsangebote klar sichtbar machen.”
Unternehmen müssen hinter den Trend blicken
Früher war es für viele undenkbar, eine Beförderung abzulehnen. Aktuelle Studien deuten allerdings darauf hin, dass genau das heute zur Norm geworden ist – besonders bei jüngeren Arbeitnehmer:innen. Dem Gefühl, das manche bei einem beängstigenden oder unerwünschten Beförderungsangebot empfinden, einen Namen zu geben, könne sich aber auch auf ihr Verhalten auswirken, so Bhargava. Ähnlich wie beim Quiet Quitting könnten Menschen den Begriff als Vorwand nutzen, um sich dem Trend anzuschließen. Trotzdem sieht auch er die Verantwortung bei den Arbeitgeber:innen. „Kluge Unternehmen sind diejenigen, die ein solches Wort als Hinweis auf einen Trend betrachten”, sagte er gegenüber Fast Company. Sie sollten seiner Meinung nach hinter die Fassade blicken und sich fragen, warum Mitarbeiter:innen einer Beförderung wirklich aus dem Weg gehen.
